title: Idę czy jadę?
note: Direct sequel to a1_motion, which handed him Ide/Idziesz/Wracam/Wracasz as chunks. This unit is the OTHER half of English 'go': jechac = travel by vehicle, against ide = on foot. That conceptual split is the unit, so it carries the intro's weight; the six-form grid is the second job. jechac is an -e/-esz verb, so the endings are literally the chcec/pic set from a1_present_e_esz -- called out as a callback to keep the load to one new thing. The ja-/je- stem alternation (jade/jada vs the middle four) is shown as a table fact ONLY, never dressed up as a rule -- there is nothing at A2 for him to derive. FENCED, must not appear: habitual jezdzic/chodzic (a2_chodzic), ALL past forms of jechac (jechalem etc.), prefixed motion verbs (przyjechac, wyjechac), and transport instrumentals (autobusem, pociagiem) which are the whole point of a2_inst_transport, the very next node -- vehicles appear here only as bare Nominative SUBJECTS (Autobus jedzie...), never as means. FORKS TAKEN (conservative path, batch rule 7): (a) the infinitive 'isc' is untaught anywhere in the course and tree.json explicitly assigns the full isc grid to a2_chodzic, so isc is not taught, not glossed and not even used as a quiz distractor here; the on-foot side of every contrast uses ONLY the two chunks already in the pool, ide and idziesz. Consequence, accepted: the discrimination is live at ja and ty only, and jedzie/jedziemy/jedziecie/jada have no on-foot partner in this unit. (b) Match reaches 12 with three verb+do-phrase rows; AGENTS warns against object phrases padding a form board, but the do-phrase IS the discrimination context here and a1_motion, the direct predecessor, built its board exactly this way. (c) jedziemy/jedziecie cannot take a noun subject, so those Uzycie items carry a destination phrase instead; every other Uzycie item has a real noun subject.

intro.title: English has one word. Polish has two.
intro.body:
English says I'm going for both of these, and never makes you say which:

- I'm going to the shop — walking, on your own two feet.
- I'm going to work — sitting in a car, a bus, a train, a tram.

Polish makes you choose, every single time. There is no neutral word.

On foot → Idę. You already have this one from Idę do sklepu.
By vehicle → Jadę. That is the new word.

The destination does not change. Both take do + the genitive, exactly as before: do sklepu, do pracy, do domu, do szkoły.
intro.body_pl: Pieszo = Idę. Pojazdem = Jadę. Po obu: do + dopełniacz.

intro.title: jechać — the full grid
intro.body:
The dictionary form is jechać — to go by vehicle. Here are all six persons.

Read the two shapes straight off the table: ja- in jadę and jadą, je- in the four in the middle. That is simply how the word is built. Learn the table; there is nothing to work out.
intro.body_pl: Bezokolicznik: jechać. Dwa kształty: ja- (jadę, jadą), je- (środek tabeli).

intro.title: The endings are ones you already own
intro.body:
jechać belongs to the -ę/-esz class — the same class as chcieć and pić. Line them up and the endings are identical:

chcę · chcesz · chce · chcemy · chcecie · chcą
jadę · jedziesz · jedzie · jedziemy · jedziecie · jadą

-ę · -esz · -e · -emy · -ecie · -ą

So there is only one new thing to hold: the stem swaps between ja- and je-. The endings are old news.
intro.body_pl: jechać = klasa -ę/-esz, jak chcieć i pić. Końcówki te same, zmienia się tylko temat: ja- / je-.

intro.title: Vehicles travel too
intro.body:
A bus or a train is a he/she/it, so it takes jedzie — the same form as tata jedzie.

Watch how the choice works in real sentences. Nothing about the destination tells you which verb to use; only how the person travels does.

examples.en: The bus is going to the centre.
The tram is going to the city.
Dad is going to work. (he drives)
I'm going to the shop. (I walk)
The children are going to the park. (by bus)

match.en: I'm going to the shop (on foot)

quiz.prompt: I'm going to work — I take the bus →
quiz.explain: Polish picks the verb by how you travel, not by where you are going. A bus has wheels, so it is jadę. The do-phrase after it is unchanged.
On your own two feet it is always idę, however far away the shop is. Distance is irrelevant — only the vehicle matters.
tata is a he, and the he-slot in this class takes plain -e — the same slot that gives chce and pije.
jadą is the second of the two ja- forms. The je- shape covers the middle of the table only; the outer two, jadę and jadą, keep ja-.
The ja-form is one of the two that keep ja-. The ending -ę is right; the stem is not.
The mirror of the last one: ty is inside the je- block, so the stem is je-, not ja-.

quiz.prompt: to go by vehicle — dictionary form →
quiz.explain: The dictionary form has an -ch- that never survives into the present tense — jechać, but jadę and jedziesz. Nothing to derive; the grid is the thing to know.

quiz.prompt: Are you going to the shop? — you walk there →

quiz.explain: A bus is an it, and it sits in the same slot as he and she — so the form is jedzie. The bus is the one doing the travelling, so it is the subject.

type_items.explain: Only two forms keep the ja- shape, and this is one of them. The other is jadą.
The -esz ending is the one you already use in chcesz and pijesz — this class always has it. What is new is the je- stem.
Back to ja-. The table starts and ends with the ja- shape and has je- in between.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Dad is going to work. (he drives)
Type: Mum is going to the shop. (she drives)
Type: I'm going to the shop. (I walk)
use_items.explain: Same shop, different verb from the sentence above. Polish is not asking where you are going — it is asking whether your feet or your wheels are doing the work.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: The bus is going to the centre.
Type: The train is going to the city.
Type: My brother is going to school. (by bus)
Type: Grandma is going to the pharmacy. (by car)
Type: The children are going to the park. (by bus)
use_items.explain: dzieci is plural, so the verb is the they-form jadą — the ja- shape again.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: My parents are going home. (by car)
Type: Are you going to work? (by car)
Type: Are you going to work? (on foot)
use_items.explain: The pair to the question above. Only the verb tells your listener whether you are walking or driving — nothing else in the sentence carries that.

use_items.prompt_en: Type: Today I'm going to the office. (by car)
Type: We're going to the hotel. (by car)
Type: Are you (plural) going to the bank? (by car)
